“April 12th. The balloon changed direction in a remarkable way. Although I had fully expected it, the change filled me with unmistakable delight. After following its earlier course to about twenty degrees south of the equator, it suddenly turned east at a sharp angle. It continued that way throughout the day, staying almost, if not exactly, in the plane of the moon’s elliptical orbit. One notable result of the change in course was a distinct swaying of the basket, which continued, sometimes stronger and sometimes weaker, for many hours.

“April 13th. I was badly frightened again by the same loud cracking noise that had terrified me on the tenth. I thought about it for a long time but could find no satisfactory explanation. The earth looked much smaller; seen from the balloon, its width now covered an angle of only a little more than twenty-five degrees. I could not see the moon at all, since it was almost directly overhead. I remained in the plane of its orbit but made little progress eastward.

“April 14th. The earth’s apparent width is shrinking extremely fast. Today I became strongly convinced that the balloon was traveling along the line joining the nearest and farthest points of the moon’s orbit, toward the nearest point. In other words, it was taking a direct route to meet the moon where its orbit brought it closest to earth. The moon itself was directly above me and therefore hidden from view. Compressing the air required hard and prolonged work.

“April 15th. I could no longer clearly make out even the outlines of the earth’s continents and seas. Around noon I heard, for the third time, that dreadful sound which had startled me so much before. This time it lasted several moments and grew louder as it continued. At last, as I stood dazed and terrified, expecting some horrible destruction I could not imagine, the basket shook with tremendous violence. A gigantic blazing mass of material I could not identify swept past the balloon, roaring and booming like a thousand thunderclaps. Once my fear and amazement had partly faded, I readily supposed it was an enormous piece of volcanic rock thrown out from the world I was rapidly approaching. It was probably one of those strange objects sometimes found on earth and called meteor stones for lack of a better name.

“April 16th. Today I looked upward as well as I could through each side window in turn. To my great delight, I saw a very small part of the moon’s disk extending, as it seemed, beyond the balloon’s enormous outline on every side.”

If she had known that her sister was trying to separate her from such prospects and such present pleasures, what would she have felt? Only her mother could have understood, for her feelings might have been almost the same. Lydia’s trip to Brighton was her sole consolation for the depressing certainty that her husband never meant to go there himself.

But neither of them knew what had happened, and their delight continued with scarcely a pause until the day Lydia left home.

Elizabeth was now about to see Mr. Wickham for the last time. She had often been in his company since returning, and her uneasiness had largely faded; any disturbance caused by her former affection had disappeared entirely. She had even learned to detect something affected and repetitive in the very gentleness that had first charmed her, something that now disgusted and wearied her. His current behavior toward her provided another reason for displeasure. He soon showed a desire to resume the attentions that had marked their early acquaintance, and after everything that had happened, this could only irritate her. Discovering that he had chosen her as the object of such empty, frivolous flirtation extinguished her remaining concern for him. She firmly discouraged it, while feeling the rebuke implicit in his assumption that, however long he had neglected her and for whatever reason, renewing his attentions would always flatter her vanity and win back her preference.

On the regiment’s final day in Meryton, he and several other officers dined at Longbourn. Elizabeth was so little inclined to part from him on cheerful terms that when he asked how she had spent her time at Hunsford, she mentioned that Colonel Fitzwilliam and Mr. Darcy had both stayed three weeks at Rosings, and asked whether he knew the former.

He looked surprised, displeased, and alarmed. But after a moment to collect himself, he smiled again and replied that he had often seen him in earlier days. Having remarked that he was a very gentlemanly man, he asked how she had liked him. She answered with warm approval. Soon afterward he added, with an air of indifference, “How long did you say he stayed at Rosings?”

“Nearly three weeks.”

“And you saw him often?”

“Yes, almost daily.”

“His manners are very different from his cousin’s.”

“Yes, quite different; but I think Mr. Darcy improves as one gets to know him.”

“Really!” Wickham exclaimed, with an expression she did not miss. “And may I ask—” He stopped himself, then added more cheerfully, “Is it his manner that improves?”

This brief conversation clearing matters up with Mr. Knightley gave Emma considerable pleasure. It was one of the pleasant memories of the ball that she went walking on the lawn the next morning to enjoy. She was extremely glad they had reached such a good understanding about the Eltons and held such similar opinions of both husband and wife. His praise of Harriet, his admission in her favor, was especially satisfying. The Eltons’ insolence, which for a few minutes had threatened to spoil the rest of her evening, had led to some of its greatest pleasures; and she anticipated another happy consequence—the end of Harriet’s infatuation. Harriet’s way of speaking about the incident before they left the ballroom had given her strong hopes. It was as though her eyes had suddenly opened and she could see that Mr. Elton was not the superior being she had imagined. The fever had passed, and Emma had little reason to fear that harmful politeness would set her pulse racing again. She trusted the Eltons’ ill will to provide whatever further lesson in pointed neglect might be needed. With Harriet sensible, Frank Churchill not excessively in love, and Mr. Knightley unwilling to quarrel with her, what a happy summer lay ahead!

She would not see Frank Churchill that morning. He had told her he could not indulge himself with a stop at Hartfield, since he needed to reach home by midday. She felt no regret.

Having settled all these matters in her mind, examined them, and put them in proper order, she was just turning toward the house, her spirits refreshed for the demands of the two little boys and their grandfather, when the great iron carriage gate opened. Two people entered whom she could hardly have been less prepared to see together: Frank Churchill, with Harriet leaning on his arm—Harriet herself! One moment was enough to show her that something extraordinary had happened. Harriet looked pale and frightened, and he was trying to comfort her. The iron gates were less than twenty yards from the front door; soon all three were in the hall, where Harriet immediately sank into a chair and fainted.

A young woman who faints must be revived; questions must be answered, and surprises explained. Such incidents are very interesting, but the uncertainty surrounding them cannot continue long. Within a few minutes Emma knew the whole story.

Miss Smith and Miss Bickerton, another resident pupil at Mrs. Goddard’s who had also attended the ball, had gone walking together. They had chosen the Richmond road, which seemed busy enough to be safe but had brought them into a frightening situation. About half a mile beyond Highbury, the road turned sharply and, deeply shaded by elms on either side, became very secluded for a considerable distance. When the young women had gone some way along this stretch, they suddenly noticed a group of Gypsies a short distance ahead, on a wider patch of grass beside the road.
